meta.description: Credited to Jane Austen, but it is in none of her books — we searched all eight, word for word — and no one has ever produced a source for it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are as many forms of love as there are moments in time'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Austen. The sentence appears in none of her novels, in no Wikiquote page, and in no newspaper archive we could search.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — an unsourced modern line
answer.sourceLine: This does not come from Austen. We searched the complete Project Gutenberg texts of all six novels plus Lady Susan and Love and Freindship and the sentence is absent, as is the phrase “forms of love” in any construction. It is also absent from her Wikiquote page ↗ and from Wikiquote as a whole, and no one we can find has produced a source for it.

source.heading: What the books actually say

docMeta.dd: All six novels, plus Lady Susan and Love and Freindship

source.excerpt: “There are as many forms of love as there are moments in time.”
trail: We searched the complete Project Gutenberg texts of Pride and Prejudice ↗, Emma ↗, Sense and Sensibility, Mansfield Park, Northanger Abbey, Persuasion, Lady Susan and Love and Freindship, with line breaks flattened so nothing could hide across a line ending. Neither the sentence nor the phrase “forms of love” occurs in any of them.
A search across the whole of Wikiquote returns no page containing the phrase, and Austen’s own Wikiquote page ↗ does not list it in either its sourced sections or its Misattributed section.

A search of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America newspaper archive for “as many forms of love as there are moments” returns zero results, so the sentence has no traceable print history in American newspapers through 1963.
source.excerptNote: No context to show, and that is itself informative: unlike most Austen misquotations, this one is not even a rewording of something she wrote. There is no underlying passage it could have drifted from.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About the woman on the graphic
author.bio: Jane Austen wrote six novels between 1811 and 1817, four published in her lifetime. Her subject was courtship conducted under economic pressure, and her prose is famously exact — which is what makes this sentence so obviously not hers. She wrote about a particular woman’s particular problem; abstractions about love in general are the register of a greetings card, not of Persuasion.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Austen is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for romantic aphorisms. This one carries her name almost everywhere it appears, and a source almost nowhere.

items.why: Absent from all eight of her published works — we searched the Project Gutenberg texts ↗ directly — and absent from her Wikiquote page ↗.
Unlike most Austen misquotations, this one is rarely attached to a specific book, which is a strong sign that no one repeating it has ever checked.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence has no known author. What can be stated flatly is who did not write it: the complete texts ↗ are free to read and search, and it is in none of them.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The tell here is the abstraction. Austen almost never writes about love in general — she writes about what a specific woman can afford to feel, given her income and her sisters. A sentence that treats love as a countable category belongs to a much later, much vaguer tradition.
It is worth saying that no harm was intended by anyone in this chain. A pleasant line needed an author; Austen is the name English-language readers attach to anything said gracefully about the heart.
context.pull: Austen wrote about what a specific woman could afford to feel. Not about love in general.
